chunks: What is a mux. The question: What is a mux?
A mux, short for multiplexer, is a switch controlled by digital signals. It has several data inputs, a few select inputs, and one output.
The select inputs, read as a binary number, choose which data input gets passed to the output.
Think of the input selector knob on an old stereo, with positions for CD, tape and radio. Whatever position the knob points to is what you hear, and the other sources are ignored.
A mux is that knob, except the knob position is a number written in 0 seconds and 1 seconds instead of an angle.
A 2:1 mux from gates. The inverter makes the S' signal that enables A, and S itself enables B; the OR merges the two (only one AND output can be 1 at a time).
Notice that S' is made by an extra gate, so S' arrives one inverter delay later than S. That delay is the origin of the glitch discussed below.
Data inputs: the signals you choose between. Select lines: the control inputs that pick which data input reaches the output.
Binary number: a number written with only 0 seconds and 1 seconds. Two select lines give 4 combinations, so they can choose among 4 inputs ("Converting between number bases").
Start with the smallest mux: 2 inputs, A and B, and one select line S. If S is 0, the output Y copies A. If S is 1, Y copies B. Suppose A is 1 and B is 0.
With S = 0 the output is 1, and with S = 1 the output is 0. Now make it a 4-input mux. It needs two select lines, because two lines give 4 combinations.
Select 10 (binary for 2) and the output copies the input numbered 2, counting from 0. That is the whole idea: select lines pick one input and the output copies it.
"A mux is a digitally controlled switch: N data inputs, log-two-of-N select lines, one output that follows whichever input the select picks.
A 2-to-1 is Y equals not-S times A plus S times B, so an inverter, two ANDs and an OR, or just two transmission gates in CMOS. You can tree them to make bigger ones.
They're used for register source selection, ALU result select, and every if-else in RTL.
They're also universal: tie the data inputs to constants and you've got a look-up table, which is what an FPGA is built from."
